concepts.name: The agent loop, turns and the result message
Custom tools through an in-process MCP server
Allowed tools, disallowed tools and permission modes
Hooks that allow, deny or change tool calls

questions.prompt: In the Claude Agent SDK, when does the agent loop end on its own?

choices.text: After 10 turns, the default `max_turns`, whatever Claude is doing
After each tool call, when control returns to your code to continue
When Claude replies with no tool calls; the SDK then yields a `ResultMessage`
When the context window is full and no more messages can be added

questions.explanation: The loop repeats: Claude responds, the SDK runs any requested tools and feeds the results back. It ends when Claude produces a response with no tool calls, followed by a `ResultMessage` with the final text, usage, cost and session ID. `max_turns` has no limit by default, and when the context fills up the SDK compacts it instead of stopping.

sources.title: How the agent loop works
sources.claim: The loop repeats until Claude produces a response with no tool calls, after which the SDK yields a ResultMessage with final text, usage, cost and session ID; max_turns defaults to no limit and a nearly full context is compacted automatically.

questions.prompt: You set `max_turns=5` and the task needs more. What does the SDK give you?

choices.text: A `ResultMessage` with `subtype` `"error_max_turns"` and no `result` text
A `ResultMessage` with `subtype` `"success"` and a partial `result`
Nothing: it pauses and waits for you to raise the limit
A `MaxTurnsExceeded` exception before any result message

questions.explanation: When a limit is hit the SDK returns a `ResultMessage` with an error subtype, `error_max_turns` or `error_max_budget_usd`. The `result` field exists only on `success`, so check `subtype` first. A single-shot `query()` then also raises after yielding that result, so wrap the loop in `try`. The session ID is still there, so you can resume.

sources.title: How the agent loop works
sources.claim: Hitting max_turns yields a ResultMessage with subtype error_max_turns, whose result field is absent (only success has it); single-shot query() then raises, and session_id is still present for resuming.

questions.prompt: You register an in-process server with `mcp_servers={"files": server}`. It has a tool named `move_file`. What do you put in `allowed_tools` so it runs without a permission prompt?

choices.text: `"move_file"`
`"files.move_file"`
`"mcp_files_move_file"`
`"mcp__files__move_file"`

questions.explanation: Tools from an MCP server are named `mcp__{server_name}__{tool_name}`, and the server name is the key you used in `mcp_servers`. So the tool is `mcp__files__move_file`. To approve every tool on that server you can use `mcp__files__*`.

sources.title: Give Claude custom tools
sources.claim: The key used in mcpServers becomes the server segment of the tool name mcp__{server_name}__{tool_name}, which you list in allowedTools to skip the prompt; mcp__<server>__* covers every tool on that server.

questions.prompt: Your custom tool's handler raises an uncaught `FileNotFoundError`. What happens?

choices.text: The whole `query()` call raises `FileNotFoundError` and the agent loop stops
It becomes an error result with the raw message; Claude sees it and the loop continues
The SDK retries the tool call three times with exponential backoff, then ends the agent loop
The SDK swallows it and returns an empty successful result to Claude

questions.explanation: A handler error doesn't stop the loop: the SDK's in-process MCP server catches it and returns it as an error result carrying the raw exception message. Catching it yourself and returning `"is_error": True` with a composed message is better, because you can tell Claude what failed and what to try instead.

sources.title: Give Claude custom tools
sources.claim: An uncaught handler exception is converted by the in-process MCP server into an error result carrying the raw exception message; Claude sees it and the agent loop continues.

questions.prompt: For your file-organising agent, explain how you would add a custom `classify_file` tool, let it run without prompting, and report a missing file so Claude can recover.

model_answer.summary: Define it with `@tool` and an async handler, wrap it in `create_sdk_mcp_server`, pass the server in `mcp_servers`, and list `mcp__<server>__classify_file` in `allowed_tools`. For a missing file, return a clear message with `is_error` set rather than raising.
key_points: `@tool` takes a name, a description and an input schema, and decorates an async handler
The handler returns a dict with a `content` list of blocks such as `{"type": "text", "text": ...}`
`create_sdk_mcp_server` wraps the tools in a server that runs in your own process, passed through `mcp_servers`
Adding `mcp__<server>__classify_file` to `allowed_tools` approves it without a prompt
Returning `"is_error": True` with a composed message lets Claude read what went wrong and try something else

questions.explanation: These steps come straight from the custom-tools guide. The description matters because Claude reads it to decide when to call the tool. An error result is part of the loop, not the end of it: Claude can retry, try a different tool or explain the failure.

sources.title: Give Claude custom tools
sources.claim: A tool is defined with @tool (name, description Claude reads, input schema) on an async handler returning a content list, wrapped in create_sdk_mcp_server (in-process), passed via mcp_servers, pre-approved via allowed_tools, and can return is_error True with a composed message.

questions.prompt: You set `allowed_tools=["Read"]` and `permission_mode="bypassPermissions"`. Can Claude run `Bash`?

choices.text: No: only the tools listed in `allowed_tools` are available to Claude at all
Only after your `canUseTool` callback approves it, since `Bash` isn't pre-approved
Yes: unlisted tools fall through to the permission mode, and `bypassPermissions` approves them
No: `bypassPermissions` is ignored whenever `allowed_tools` is set, so only `Read` can ever run

questions.explanation: The docs warn that `allowed_tools` does not constrain `bypassPermissions`. Unlisted tools are still available; their calls fall through to the permission mode, which approves them. To keep a tool away while bypassing prompts, list it in `disallowed_tools`. Deny rules and hooks are checked before the mode, so they still apply.

sources.title: Configure permissions
sources.claim: allowed_tools does not constrain bypassPermissions: unlisted tools fall through to the permission mode, which approves them, so allowed_tools=['Read'] with bypassPermissions still approves Bash; use disallowed_tools to block tools.

questions.prompt: You want Claude never even to attempt `Bash`. Which option does that?

choices.text: `disallowed_tools=["Bash"]`, which removes the tool from Claude's context
Leaving `Bash` out of `allowed_tools`, so it's never offered to Claude
`permission_mode="acceptEdits"`, which blocks every tool other than file edits
`disallowed_tools=["Bash(*)"]`, a wildcard rule matching every Bash command

questions.explanation: A bare tool name in `disallowed_tools` removes the tool from Claude's context, so Claude can't see or attempt it. Leaving a tool out of `allowed_tools` only means its calls go through the normal permission flow. A scoped rule like `Bash(rm *)` keeps the tool visible and denies only matching calls.

sources.title: Configure permissions
sources.claim: A bare name in disallowed_tools such as 'Bash' removes the tool definition so Claude cannot see or attempt it, while a scoped rule such as 'Bash(rm *)' keeps the tool and denies only matching calls; unlisted tools remain available.

sources.title: Give Claude custom tools
sources.claim: Tools left out of allowedTools remain available and go through the permission flow; bare-name disallowedTools entries remove the tool from Claude's context.

questions.prompt: Two `PreToolUse` hooks match the same tool call. One returns `permissionDecision: "allow"`, the other `"deny"`. What happens?

choices.text: The call runs, because the first hook to finish decides the final outcome
The call runs, because an explicit `allow` overrides any `deny`
Claude is asked to choose between the two conflicting decisions
The call is blocked: `deny` takes priority over every other decision

questions.explanation: Matching hooks run in parallel and the most restrictive result applies: `deny` beats `defer`, which beats `ask`, which beats `allow`. A single `deny` blocks the call whatever the other hooks return. Because completion order isn't fixed, each hook should work on its own.

sources.title: Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks
sources.claim: All matching hooks run in parallel and the most restrictive decision applies: deny over defer over ask over allow, so a single deny blocks the call; completion order is non-deterministic.

questions.prompt: Your file-organising agent must never move files outside `~/Downloads/inbox`. Explain where you would enforce this and why a hook is safer than relying on `allowed_tools` or a `canUseTool` callback.

model_answer.summary: Use a `PreToolUse` hook, matched to the tools that move or write files, that returns `permissionDecision: "deny"` when a path is outside the folder. Hooks run before every other permission step and a hook deny holds even in `bypassPermissions`, while `canUseTool` is skipped for auto-approved calls.
key_points: A `PreToolUse` hook with a `matcher` for the file tools (for example your `mcp__files__move_file`, or `Write|Edit`) sees each call's `tool_input`
It returns `permissionDecision: "deny"` with a reason when the path is outside the allowed folder
Hooks run first in the permission order, and a hook deny applies even in `bypassPermissions` mode
`allowed_tools` only pre-approves tools and doesn't restrict their arguments
`canUseTool` is never called for a call already approved by an allow rule or the permission mode

questions.explanation: The permissions page puts hooks at the top of the evaluation order and says that auto-approved calls never reach `canUseTool`, so checks placed there can be silently bypassed. For a check that must run on every call, it recommends a `PreToolUse` hook. The denial goes back to Claude as the tool result, so the agent can try another path.

sources.title: Configure permissions
sources.claim: Hooks run first in the evaluation order, a hook deny applies even in bypassPermissions, allow rules only pre-approve, and calls auto-approved by a mode or allow rule never reach canUseTool, so the page recommends a PreToolUse hook for checks on every call.

sources.title: Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks
sources.claim: PreToolUse hooks use a matcher on tool names (e.g. 'Write|Edit'), read tool_input, and can return permissionDecision 'deny' with permissionDecisionReason, which tells the model why.

questions.prompt: A programmatic subagent (not a fork) is started through the `Agent` tool. What does it receive from the parent?

choices.text: The parent's full conversation history and tool results, so it can pick up where it left off
Its `AgentDefinition.prompt` and the prompt passed to the `Agent` tool; no parent history
The parent's system prompt and tool list, but none of the conversation so far
Nothing up front: it must read the parent's transcript file to learn its task

questions.explanation: A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context: its own system prompt from `AgentDefinition.prompt`, the prompt string the parent passed to the `Agent` tool, its tool definitions and project CLAUDE.md if settings load it. It does not get the parent's history or system prompt, so put any file paths or decisions it needs in that prompt. (The tool was named `Task` in older Claude Code versions.)

sources.title: Subagents in the SDK
sources.claim: A non-fork subagent receives its AgentDefinition.prompt, the Agent tool's prompt, tool definitions and project CLAUDE.md, but not the parent's conversation history, tool results or system prompt; the tool was named Task in tool_use blocks before Claude Code v2.1.63.

questions.prompt: Your agent must scan 500 files and sort them into folders. Explain why you would hand the scan to a subagent, what you must put in the delegation prompt, and how you would limit what the subagent can do.

model_answer.summary: A subagent keeps the scan's many tool calls in its own context and returns only its final message, so the main conversation stays small. Because the delegation prompt is its only input from the parent, it must carry the paths and rules, and the `tools` field limits it to what it needs.
key_points: Context isolation: intermediate tool calls and results stay in the subagent; only its final message returns to the parent
The `Agent` tool's prompt is the only thing passed from parent to subagent, so include folder paths, rules and decisions in it
`AgentDefinition.tools` restricts the subagent to the listed tools, such as `Read`, `Glob` and `Grep`
The `description` tells Claude when to use the subagent, so it should be specific

questions.explanation: The subagents guide lists context isolation, parallel runs, specialised instructions and tool restrictions as the benefits. A tool left out of `tools` isn't in the subagent's session at all. Subagents can spawn their own subagents, and the budget cap (`max_budget_usd`) counts their spend too.

sources.title: Subagents in the SDK
sources.claim: Subagents give context isolation (only the final message returns), parallelization, specialized instructions and tool restrictions; the Agent tool prompt is the only parent-to-subagent input, tools limits the subagent's tools, description guides when Claude uses it, subagents can nest, and max_budget_usd counts their spend.
